claims.text: The initial material is a bulk, coarse-grained, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi alloy made by conventional casting or additive manufacturing.
High-pressure torsion at room or cryogenic temperature can refine CoCrFeMnNi into an ultra-nanocrystalline matrix.
High-pressure torsion followed by annealing at 300–400 °C produces dynamically amorphized grain boundaries in bulk CoCrFeMnNi.
An accumulated shear strain greater than 10 is required to generate the proposed microstructure.
In-situ TEM monitoring during annealing can ensure grain-boundary amorphization without excessive grain growth.
Annealing within 300–400 °C preserves the nanoscale structure and prevents significant grain coarsening.
Annealing above 400 °C or applying insufficient shear strain prevents dynamic amorphization and its mechanical benefits.
Highly refined, near-amorphous CoCrFeMnNi formed by severe shear can exhibit inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
The cited inverse Hall–Petch and near-amorphous structure extends from a highly deformed near-surface tribological layer to the bulk grain-boundary network proposed here.
At ultra-small grain sizes, conventional dislocation-mediated strengthening is replaced by grain-boundary-dominated deformation.
Low-temperature annealing partially recovers the lattice while retaining a softened amorphous grain-boundary layer.
The amorphous grain-boundary layer increases strength by impeding dislocation motion.
The amorphous grain-boundary layer maintains ductility by enabling shear banding.
The amorphous grain-boundary layer improves fracture resistance through crack blunting.
The processed alloy will have approximately 20–30% greater yield strength than conventionally processed coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi.
The processing route will maintain or improve ductility relative to the coarse-grained baseline.
The processing route will enhance Young's modulus relative to the coarse-grained baseline.
The processing route will improve fracture resistance relative to the coarse-grained baseline.
